---
title: "Development loop"
description: "Set up OmicsBase for development, change the notes app or the engine, run the tests and preview these docs."
---

This page shows three ways to work on OmicsBase. Pick the one that fits your change:

- **Change the web pages only** (React components, styles, texts): run the page dev server against a local install. See [Work on the web pages](#ui).
- **Change the server or the engine**: build the images and run the full stack from source. See [Run the full stack from source](#from-source).
- **Change Reports, or test your images before a release**: run the local install with your own images. See [Run the local install with your own images](#own-images).

## What you need {#requirements}

- Git.
- Docker Engine with Compose v2.
- Node.js 24 and npm. The LibreChat fork names its version in `librechat/.nvmrc`.
- Python 3.12 or later.
- Quarto 1.11 or later, if you work on these docs.
- Your own key for at least one model provider.

The images are built for Linux on Intel/AMD (amd64). The engine image installs a large R and Bioconductor stack, so its first build takes a long time and needs plenty of disk space.

## Get the source {#clone}

1. Clone the repository with both submodules:

   ```bash
   git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/0xMuluh/omicsbase.git
   ```

2. Go into it:

   ```bash
   cd omicsbase
   ```

3. Check that both submodules are filled:

   ```bash
   git submodule status
   ```

   You should see two lines, one for `librechat` and one for `openhands`, each starting with a commit.

If you cloned without `--recurse-submodules`, run `git submodule update --init --recursive` now.

## Work on the web pages {#ui}

The page dev server (Vite) serves the web pages from your source and reloads them when you save a file. It sends every `/api` and `/oauth` request on to a running LibreChat server. The quickest such server is a local install.

1. Install OmicsBase on your machine as described in [Install on your own machine](../self-host/install.qmd). Its server listens on port 3080.
2. Open <http://localhost:3080> and create your account.
3. In your clone, go into the fork:

   ```bash
   cd librechat
   ```

4. Install the packages:

   ```bash
   npm ci
   ```

5. Build the shared packages that the pages import:

   ```bash
   npm run build:packages
   ```

6. Start the dev server and point it at port 3080:

   ```bash
   BACKEND_PORT=3080 npm run frontend:dev
   ```

   You should see Vite report its address:

   ```text
   ➜  Local:   http://localhost:3090/
   ```

7. Open <http://localhost:3090> and sign in with the account from step 2.

<!-- screenshot: dev-server-notes — the notes app served by the Vite dev server on localhost:3090 -->

Changes under `client/src/` show up in the browser when you save. Changes to the server (`api/`, `packages/api/`) do not: the server is the one in the install's image. For those, use the full stack below.

If you change a shared package (`packages/data-provider`, `packages/client`, …), run `npm run build:packages` again.

## Run the full stack from source {#from-source}

This runs the same Compose stack as production, with images you build yourself.

### 1. Copy the settings {#from-source-config}

1. From the repository root, copy the three templates into the fork:

   ```bash
   cp .env.example librechat/.env
   cp deployment/librechat.yaml librechat/librechat.yaml
   cp deployment/docker-compose.override.yml librechat/docker-compose.override.yml
   ```

2. Open `librechat/.env` in an editor.
3. Set `UID` and `GID` to your own ids. `id -u` and `id -g` print them.
4. Give each of these a different random value: `JWT_SECRET`, `JWT_REFRESH_SECRET`, `ADMIN_PANEL_SESSION_SECRET`, `MEILI_MASTER_KEY`, `OMICSBASE_AUTH_SECRET` and `CREDS_KEY`. This command prints one value each time you run it:

   ```bash
   openssl rand -hex 32
   ```

5. Set `CREDS_IV` to the output of `openssl rand -hex 16`.
6. Set `ALLOW_REGISTRATION=true`, so you can create the first account. Set it back to `false` afterwards if others can reach your machine.
7. Add the key of each model provider you want to use.
8. Open `librechat/librechat.yaml`.
9. Remove the endpoints you have no key for.
10. Under `mcpServers`, change the `url` of `notethreads` to the engine in your stack:

    ```yaml
    url: http://engine:8001/sse
    ```

    Keep its `headers` and `requiresOAuth: false` lines.

Keep `.env`, keys, databases and project files out of Git.

### 2. Prepare the folders {#from-source-dirs}

1. Create the folders the stack writes to. The script uses `sudo`:

   ```bash
   scripts/prepare_runtime_dirs.sh
   ```

   It ends with:

   ```text
   Runtime directories prepared.
   ```

### 3. Build the images {#from-source-build}

Use the same Docker context for building and starting. A Docker *context* names which Docker engine a command talks to; `default` is the one on your machine.

1. Build the LibreChat image:

   ```bash
   python3 scripts/build_librechat.py --context default
   ```

   It ends with the tag it built, named after the fork's commit:

   ```text
   Built omicsbase-librechat:<commit>; running containers were not changed.
   ```

2. In `librechat/.env`, set `OMICSBASE_LIBRECHAT_IMAGE` to that tag.
3. Build the engine. This builds `omicsbase-engine:dev` from `engine/Dockerfile`. The build needs the knowledge index `engine/knowledge/knowledge.db`, which is not in git, so copy it from the published image first:

   ```bash
   python3 scripts/fetch_knowledge_db.py ghcr.io/0xmuluh/omicsbase-engine:latest
   python3 scripts/build_engine.py --context default
   ```

   It ends with:

   ```text
   Built omicsbase-engine:dev. Running containers and deployment configuration were not changed.
   ```

Building never restarts running containers.

### 4. Build the knowledge index {#from-source-knowledge}

1. Download the books and build `engine/knowledge/knowledge.db`, using the engine image:

   ```bash
   docker --context default run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp \
     -v "$PWD:/app" --entrypoint python3 omicsbase-engine:dev /app/scripts/setup_knowledge.py
   ```

   It prints one `Fetched …` line per book, then:

   ```text
   Installed <n> chunks from <n> books at …/engine/knowledge/knowledge.db
   ```

The stack mounts `engine/` into the engine container, so the engine sees the new index without a rebuild. The books keep their own licences; see `knowledge/ATTRIBUTION.md`. `knowledge/README.md` shows how to run the same script without Docker.

### 5. Start the stack {#from-source-start}

1. Check the Compose files:

   ```bash
   docker --context default compose --project-directory "$PWD/librechat" \
     --env-file librechat/.env -p librechat \
     -f librechat/docker-compose.yml -f librechat/docker-compose.override.yml config --quiet
   ```

   It prints nothing when the files are valid.

2. Start the services:

   ```bash
   docker --context default compose --project-directory "$PWD/librechat" \
     --env-file librechat/.env -p librechat \
     -f librechat/docker-compose.yml -f librechat/docker-compose.override.yml up -d
   ```

3. Open <http://localhost:3080>.
4. Create your account.
5. Open a new note and ask for a small R calculation, to check that notes run.

Ports 3000, 3080 and 8001 must be free. Containers with the same names must not belong to another stack.

In this stack the Reports page says Reports is not set up, because no router runs here. To work on Reports, use [your own images in the local install](#own-images).

### Apply a change {#from-source-changes}

| You changed | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| A server file listed under `volumes` in `docker-compose.override.yml` (for example `api/server/routes/notes.js`) | Recreate the `api` service: add `up -d --force-recreate api` to the Compose command above. The file is mounted from your checkout, so no rebuild is needed. |
| Python code in `engine/` | Restart the engine: `docker restart omicsbase-engine`. The folder is mounted into the container. |
| Anything else in `librechat/` (`packages/`, `client/`) | Rebuild with `build_librechat.py`, set the new tag in `.env`, and recreate `api`. |
| R packages in `engine/image/r-package-list.R` | Rebuild with `build_engine.py` and recreate `engine`. |

## Run the local install with your own images {#own-images}

The local install takes its images from `ghcr.io/0xmuluh/` with the tag in `OMICSBASE_VERSION`. If an image with that name and tag exists on your machine, Compose uses it. Tag your builds `dev` to slip them in.

1. Build the engine, as in [Build the images](#from-source-build).
2. Build the Reports image. It is built on top of `omicsbase-engine:dev`:

   ```bash
   python3 scripts/build_openhands.py --context default
   ```

   It installs the interface's packages, runs its contract tests, type-checks and builds it, then ends with:

   ```text
   Built omicsbase-openhands:dev; running containers were not changed.
   ```

3. Build the LibreChat image, as in [Build the images](#from-source-build).
4. Give the three images the names the local install uses:

   ```bash
   docker tag omicsbase-engine:dev ghcr.io/0xmuluh/omicsbase-engine:dev
   docker tag omicsbase-openhands:dev ghcr.io/0xmuluh/omicsbase-reports:dev
   docker tag omicsbase-librechat:<commit> ghcr.io/0xmuluh/omicsbase-librechat:dev
   ```

5. In your install's `.env` (by default `~/omicsbase/.env`), set:

   ```text
   OMICSBASE_VERSION=dev
   ```

6. In the install folder, start it again:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d
   ```

To go back to the published images, set `OMICSBASE_VERSION=latest` in the same `.env` and run `install.sh` again. While it says `dev`, `install.sh` stops at the download step, because no `dev` images are published.

## Run the tests {#tests}

### Python tests {#tests-python}

1. From the repository root, run the tests for the Reports gateway, the router and the knowledge setup. They need `pytest`, `fastapi`, `httpx` and `PyJWT`:

   ```bash
   python3 -m pytest tests
   ```

   The last line counts the results, for example:

   ```text
   33 passed
   ```

2. Run the engine tests inside the engine image, which has the engine's Python packages and R:

   ```bash
   docker run --rm -v "$PWD/engine:/app/engine" --entrypoint python3 omicsbase-engine:dev \
     -m unittest discover -s /app/engine/tests -t /app
   ```

   It ends with `OK` when all tests pass. `test_execution_latency.py` and `test_kernel_limits.py` start real R sessions, so they take a while. None of the tests call a model.

### LibreChat fork tests {#tests-librechat}

The fork uses Jest, a JavaScript test runner. Run these in `librechat/`, after `npm ci` and `npm run build:packages`.

1. Test the server package, which holds the notes and Reports code:

   ```bash
   npm run test:packages:api
   ```

2. Test the web pages:

   ```bash
   npm run test:client
   ```

To run one test file, call Jest in its package. For example:

```bash
cd packages/api
npx jest src/projects/roihu.spec.ts
```

### OpenHands fork tests {#tests-openhands}

1. From the repository root, run the contract tests without building an image:

   ```bash
   python3 scripts/build_openhands.py --verify-only
   ```

   It ends with:

   ```text
   Verification complete (vitest contract tests passed).
   ```

## Lint rules in the LibreChat fork {#lint}

The fork checks its code and design rules with ESLint, a code checker. The rules are in `eslint.config.mjs`. These come up most often:

- **No inline styles.** `style={{…}}` is reported, except for measured geometry such as `width`, `height`, `top`, `transform` and `zIndex`. Use theme classes.
- **No arbitrary Tailwind values.** Classes such as `w-[37px]` or `text-[#333]` are reported, except for layout. Use the theme's scale.
- **No raw colours.** Use the theme's colour classes.

To lint the whole fork:

```bash
npm run lint
```

A Git hook runs the same checks on the files you commit. It runs `node` and `npx` from your `PATH`, and its checks need Node 24. With an older Node first on your `PATH`, the commit fails. If you use nvm, run `nvm use` in `librechat/` first; it reads `.nvmrc`.

## Preview these docs {#docs}

1. Go into the docs folder:

   ```bash
   cd docs
   ```

2. Start the preview:

   ```bash
   quarto preview
   ```

   Quarto opens the site in your browser and reloads a page when you save it.

<!-- screenshot: docs-preview — the docs site served by quarto preview, with the sidebar open on Develop -->

CI and `scripts/publish_docs.sh` render with the `publish` profile (`quarto render docs --profile publish`). That profile writes `llms.txt` and needs Quarto 1.11 or later. `changelog.qmd` is written by `scripts/build_changelog.sh`, which reads the GitHub releases with the `gh` command.
